title: Applied anatomy: liver segments, porta hepatis and the Pringle manoeuvre

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in the hepatobiliary clinic
brief.scenario: Sean Docherty, 58, has a 4 cm lesion in segment VI of the liver and is listed for resection.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the segmental anatomy of the liver and the porta hepatis, and relate them to his operation.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Functional liver first: segments by vessels, not by ligaments. Then the hilum and inflow control.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Using the falciform ligament as the right–left boundary.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "The liver has eight Couinaud segments, each with its own inflow, outflow and bile drainage."

grid.label: Functional division
grid.fail: Uses the falciform ligament as the right–left boundary.
grid.pass: Eight segments, each with its own portal pedicle, hepatic venous and biliary drainage; Cantlie's line (gallbladder fossa to IVC) divides right from left.
grid.high: The middle hepatic vein runs in Cantlie's plane; right and left hepatic veins divide each side into sections.

grid.label: Number the segments
grid.fail: Cannot say where segment VI lies.
grid.pass: I caudate; II and III left lateral; IV left medial; V and VIII right anterior; VI and VII right posterior. VI is inferior right posterior.
grid.high: Plans a segmentectomy or right posterior sectionectomy (VI and VII), preserving remnant liver.

grid.label: Caudate lobe
grid.fail: Does not know which segment is the caudate lobe.
grid.pass: Segment I: inflow from both right and left pedicles; drains by short veins straight into the IVC.
grid.high: Explains why it is spared and enlarges in Budd–Chiari syndrome.

grid.label: Hepatoduodenal ligament
grid.fail: Puts the portal vein in front.
grid.pass: Free edge of the lesser omentum: bile duct right anterior, hepatic artery left anterior, portal vein behind; epiploic foramen posterior.
grid.high: Names variants: replaced right hepatic artery from the superior mesenteric; replaced left hepatic from left gastric in the lesser omentum.

grid.label: Pringle manoeuvre
grid.fail: Describes clamping the hepatic veins or the IVC.
grid.pass: Finger through the epiploic foramen; clamp or sling the hepatoduodenal ligament to stop hepatic arterial and portal inflow.
grid.high: Bleeding despite clamping suggests hepatic venous or caval back-bleeding, or a replaced left hepatic artery.

grid.label: Ischaemia time
grid.fail: Leaves the clamp on with no time limit.
grid.pass: Intermittent clamping (for example 20 min on, 5 min off) is better tolerated than continuous, especially in abnormal liver.
grid.high: Times it aloud with the anaesthetist; accumulated clamp time over 120 min linked to more liver injury.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Into right and left lobes by the falciform ligament.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I think it's in the left lobe.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What lies in the free edge of the lesser omentum?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The portal vein at the front, then the artery and duct.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you control bleeding from the liver?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How long can the clamp stay on?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: As long as needed until the bleeding stops.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Into eight Couinaud segments, each with its own portal pedicle, hepatic venous drainage and bile duct. Cantlie's line, from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC, divides right from left.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Number them and tell me where segment VI lies.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I is the caudate. II and III are left lateral, IV left medial. V and VIII right anterior, VI and VII right posterior. VI is the inferior right posterior segment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Segment I gets inflow from both right and left pedicles and drains by short veins straight into the IVC.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What is in the hepatoduodenal ligament?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The bile duct to the right and front, the hepatic artery to the left and front, and the portal vein behind. The epiploic foramen lies behind the free edge.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I pass a finger through the epiploic foramen and clamp or sling the ligament, stopping hepatic arterial and portal inflow.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How long can it stay on?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Intermittent clamping, for example 20 minutes on and 5 off, is better tolerated than continuous, especially in an abnormal liver.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The middle hepatic vein. The right and left hepatic veins divide each side into sections.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you resect segment VI?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Segmentectomy of VI, or a right posterior sectionectomy of VI and VII, keeping as much remnant liver as possible.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why does the caudate matter clinically?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Its direct drainage into the IVC spares it in Budd–Chiari, so it enlarges.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A replaced right hepatic artery from the superior mesenteric runs behind in the ligament. A replaced left hepatic from the left gastric runs in the lesser omentum.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The clamp is on and it's still bleeding.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Inflow is controlled, so that's back-bleeding from the hepatic veins or IVC, or a replaced left hepatic artery outside the clamp.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd call out clamp times to the anaesthetist. Accumulated clamp time over 120 minutes has been linked to more liver injury.

failures.move: Dividing the liver at the falciform ligament.
failures.consequence: Plans resection lines that ignore the vessels, risking an ischaemic or congested remnant.

failures.move: Clamping hepatic veins for inflow control.
failures.consequence: Confuses inflow and outflow; risks caval injury and uncontrolled bleeding.

failures.move: Leaving the clamp on without a time limit.
failures.consequence: Ischaemia–reperfusion injury and postoperative liver failure, especially in steatotic or cirrhotic liver.

failures.move: Placing the portal vein in front.
failures.consequence: Cannot explain the approach through the epiploic foramen.

recovery.line: Caudate is I; then clockwise from the left lateral segments, II to VIII.

recovery.when: Asked about persistent bleeding with a Pringle
recovery.line: Inflow is controlled, so think hepatic veins, IVC or an aberrant artery.

knowledge.fact: Eight segments; Cantlie's line from gallbladder fossa to IVC, with the middle hepatic vein in its plane.
Caudate (I) drains directly into the IVC.
Hepatoduodenal ligament: bile duct right, hepatic artery left, portal vein behind.
Intermittent clamping (15 min on, 5 off) better tolerated than continuous, especially in abnormal liver.
Intermittent Pringle (20 on, 5 off): accumulated ischaemia over 120 min linked to more liver injury.

recall.think: Uncontrolled bleeding and liver failure from an ischaemic remnant.
do: Map segments by vessels, not ligaments
recall.trap: Falciform ligament is not the functional midline.
recall.finish: Segmental or sectional resection preserving remnant.

sources.name: Gray's Anatomy for Students (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell)
sources.supports: Couinaud segments and their vascular basis; Cantlie's line and the middle hepatic vein; caudate lobe drainage; contents and arrangement of the hepatoduodenal ligament; hepatic artery variants

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Pringle manoeuvre through the epiploic foramen; persistent bleeding despite inflow control; liver resection terminology

sources.name: Belghiti J, Noun R, Malafosse R, et al. Continuous versus intermittent portal triad clamping for liver resection: a controlled study. Ann Surg 1999;229:369–75
sources.supports: Intermittent clamping (15 min on, 5 min off) better tolerated than continuous clamping, especially in abnormal liver parenchyma

sources.name: Man K, Fan ST, Ng IO, et al. Tolerance of the liver to intermittent Pringle maneuver in hepatectomy for liver tumors. Arch Surg 1999;134:533–9
sources.supports: Intermittent Pringle of 20 min with 5 min release; accumulated ischaemic time over 120 min associated with substantial liver damage

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; examiner-led questioning in applied knowledge stations

reveals.finding: Ask the candidate to number the segments, then: which segment lies inferiorly in the right posterior section, lateral to segment V and below segment VII?
Ask: in the free edge of the lesser omentum, which structure lies posteriorly, and which lie in front of it on the right and on the left?
Bleeding from the cut surface continues after clamping.

push.question: What divides the functional right and left liver?
push.expect: Cantlie's line, gallbladder fossa to IVC, middle hepatic vein.

push.question: What is special about the caudate?
push.expect: Dual inflow; drains straight into the IVC.

push.question: How long can the Pringle stay on?
push.expect: Intermittent, for example 20 on, 5 off; time it.

curveballs.safeAnswer: Intermittent clamping, strictly timed; preserve remnant.
Remnant of the left umbilical vein, in the free edge of the falciform ligament.

curveballs.prompt: Why can a Pringle not control all liver bleeding?
curveballs.safeAnswer: It stops inflow only; hepatic veins and IVC still bleed back.
